pests.name: Carrot rust fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Rusty, reddish-brown tunnels and surface scarring honeycomb the lower root, often with the maggots present; heavy feeding stunts plants and the wounds open the door to parsnip canker. Because parsnip is in the ground a long time, late-season damage can be significant.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The lower part of the root gets rusty, reddish-brown tunnels and scars, sometimes with small maggots inside. Bad damage stunts the plant and lets root rot get in. Because parsnips sit in the ground for months, the damage can build up.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of the carrot rust fly (carrot fly), a small fly whose maggots mine the roots of carrot-family crops. There are typically two or more generations a season, and damage worsens the longer roots stay in the ground. (USU Extension; RHS)
pests.cause_beginner: The maggots of the carrot rust fly (also called carrot fly), a small fly whose young tunnel into carrot-family roots. There are usually two or more rounds a year, and the longer the roots are in the ground, the worse it gets. (USU Extension; RHS)
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no rescue for tunneled roots; management is preventive. Lift damaged roots and do not leave culls in the bed, and harvest before late-season generations build. Naturally occurring controls and good rotation reduce pressure.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: You cannot fix roots that are already tunneled, so this is about prevention. Pull and remove damaged roots, do not leave leftovers in the bed, and harvest before the late-season flies build up.
pests.prevention_seasoned: A floating row cover or fine insect mesh laid over the bed at sowing keeps the egg-laying flies off and is the most effective home defense. (RHS) Rotate parsnips away from where carrot-family crops grew, avoid leaving roots in the ground longer than needed where pressure is high, and time sowings to dodge peak fly flights.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover the bed with a fine insect mesh or row cover right after sowing to keep the flies from laying eggs. This is the best home defense. (RHS) Move parsnips away from where carrots or their relatives grew, and do not leave roots in the ground longer than you need to where this pest is bad.

pests.name: Leafminers
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Pale, winding tunnels or blotches appear inside the leaves where the larvae feed between the leaf surfaces. On parsnip, grown for the root, this is mostly cosmetic and rarely affects the harvest unless young plants are heavily mined.
pests.symptoms_beginner: You will see pale, squiggly trails or blotchy patches inside the leaves, where the little larvae feed between the top and bottom of the leaf. Since you eat the parsnip root, not the leaves, this is mostly a looks problem.
pests.cause_seasoned: The larvae of leafmining flies that tunnel within the foliage of carrot-family and other crops. Several generations can occur in a season. (USU Extension)
pests.cause_beginner: The young of small leafmining flies that tunnel inside the leaves. They can have several rounds in a season. (USU Extension)
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Pick off and destroy mined leaves as they appear, which removes the larvae; sprays are largely ineffective because the larvae are protected inside the leaf. Vigorous plants outgrow light damage.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off and throw away (do not compost) leaves with trails in them, which gets rid of the larvae. Sprays usually do not work because the pest is tucked inside the leaf, and healthy plants grow past light damage.
pests.prevention_seasoned: A floating row cover excludes the egg-laying flies, and clearing crop debris and weed hosts reduces carryover. Removing the first mined leaves promptly breaks the cycle.
pests.prevention_beginner: A row cover keeps the flies off, and clearing old leaves and weeds nearby cuts down the pest. Pulling off the first trailed leaves you see helps too.

pests.name: Aster leafhopper (aster yellows vector)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: The leafhopper itself does little direct feeding damage; the concern is that it transmits aster yellows. Plants infected by way of the leafhopper show yellowed, twisted, bunchy tops and slender, hairy, bitter roots (see the aster yellows disease entry).
pests.symptoms_beginner: The little hopping insect does not do much direct damage itself. The problem is that it carries the aster yellows disease from plant to plant, which makes the tops yellow, twisted, and bunched and the roots thin, hairy, and bitter (see the aster yellows entry).
pests.cause_seasoned: The aster leafhopper, a small wedge-shaped insect that moves the aster yellows phytoplasma between plants as it feeds. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension; USU Extension)
pests.cause_beginner: The aster leafhopper, a small insect that spreads the aster yellows disease as it feeds from plant to plant. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension; USU Extension)
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Controlling the leafhopper to prevent aster yellows is generally not effective and not recommended; the practical response is to remove infected plants and weed reservoirs promptly. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Trying to spray the leafhoppers to stop aster yellows usually does not work and is not recommended. Instead, pull out infected plants and weedy hosts right away. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)
pests.prevention_seasoned: Remove infected plants and nearby broadleaf weeds such as dandelion that harbor the phytoplasma, and a floating row cover can reduce leafhopper access to a small planting. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)
pests.prevention_beginner: Pull out infected plants and weeds like dandelions that hold the disease, and a row cover can help keep the hoppers off a small bed. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)

diseases.name: Itersonilia canker (parsnip canker)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Reddish-brown, black, or purple-black cankers form mainly on the crown and shoulders of the root, and other microbes may follow until the whole root collapses in rot. Leaves can show small orange to brown lesions with a pale green halo. Disease is worst on late-harvested crops. (UMass)
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Brown, black, or purple-black rotten patches form mostly on the crown and shoulders (the top) of the root, and the rot can spread until the whole root is ruined. Leaves can get small orange-brown spots with a pale halo. It is worst on roots left late in the season. (UMass)
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Itersonilia perplexans, also called black canker, favored by cool, wet weather. Carrot rust fly larvae predispose roots to infection by wounding them, and exposed shoulders are an entry point. (UMass)
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus (Itersonilia perplexans, also called black canker) that thrives in cool, wet weather. Carrot rust fly maggots make it worse by wounding the roots, and root tops sticking out of the soil let it in. (UMass)
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure for infected roots, and fungicide sprays do not control root cankers. Lift and use sound roots, and discard rotted ones; management is preventive and cultural. (UMass)
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a root has it, and sprays do not work on root canker. Dig and use the good roots and throw out the rotten ones. The fix is in how you grow the next crop. (UMass)
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties (Avonresister, Cobham Improved Marrow), rotate out of the carrot family for two to three years, hill soil over the shoulders through the season, control carrot rust fly, avoid waterlogged beds, harvest before very late in cold wet spells, and bury old parsnip residue by deep cultivation to lower inoculum. (UMass)
diseases.prevention_beginner: Grow a canker-resistant variety, do not plant parsnips or their relatives in the same bed for two to three years, mound a little soil over the root shoulders during the season, keep carrot rust fly down, avoid soggy soil, and clear and bury old parsnip plants after harvest. (UMass)

diseases.name: Aster yellows
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Infected plants show yellowed, reddened, twisted, and bunchy tops, and the taproot stays slender and grows a mass of fine hairy rootlets; affected roots often taste bitter. There is no cure. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Infected plants get yellow or reddish, twisted, bunched-up tops, and the root stays thin and grows a beard of fine hairy roots, often tasting bitter. There is no cure. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)
diseases.cause_seasoned: The aster yellows phytoplasma, a bacterium-like organism that lives in the plant's phloem and is spread plant to plant by the aster leafhopper. It also infects many weeds and ornamentals that serve as reservoirs. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)
diseases.cause_beginner: A bacteria-like organism (a phytoplasma) carried from plant to plant by the aster leafhopper. It also lives in many weeds and flowers, which act as a source. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure. Remove plants suspected of infection promptly, including weed hosts such as dandelion, to limit spread; trying to control the leafhopper vector is generally ineffective. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure. Pull out any plant you think is infected, plus weeds like dandelions, to slow the spread. Spraying the insect that carries it usually does not help. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Keep down broadleaf weeds that host the phytoplasma, remove infected plants as soon as they are spotted, and use a floating row cover on small plantings to reduce leafhopper access. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep weeds down, pull infected plants right away, and use a row cover on a small bed to keep the leafhoppers off. (Wisconsin Horticulture Extension)

diseases.name: Damping-off
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Seeds fail to emerge, or the slow young seedlings topple and collapse with a dark, water-soaked, pinched spot at the stem base. Losses show as bare gaps in the row. Parsnip's long germination prolongs the vulnerable window the pathogens exploit.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Seeds that never come up, or tiny seedlings that flop over and die with a dark, pinched, wet-looking spot at the base of the stem. You see it as bare gaps in the row. Because parsnips are so slow to sprout, they are exposed to this for a long time.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne pathogens, chiefly Pythium and Rhizoctonia species, favored by cool, wet, poorly drained soil and overwatering. Old or weak seed and a crusted, slow-draining seedbed increase losses.
diseases.cause_beginner: Soil organisms (mostly Pythium and Rhizoctonia) that attack sprouting seeds and baby seedlings, worst in cool, soggy, poorly drained soil and when you overwater. Old seed and a hard, wet seedbed make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Affected seedlings cannot be saved. If it appears, stop watering and let the surface dry somewhat, and clear collapsed seedlings; there is no home cure once it takes hold, so prevention is the lever.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Seedlings that have flopped will not recover. If it shows up, stop watering for a bit to let the surface dry, and clear away the fallen seedlings. There is no good home cure, so this one is about prevention.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Sow fresh seed into warm-enough (about 50°F), well-drained soil rather than cold, wet ground, keep the seedbed evenly moist without saturating it, do not sow too deep, and improve drainage or use raised beds on heavy soil.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Use fresh seed, wait until the soil is warm enough (about 50°F) and not cold and soggy, keep the seedbed damp but not soaking, do not plant too deep, and improve drainage or use a raised bed on heavy soil.
